subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a fair and equitable redistribution of Ontario ridings is now a task of immense magnitude, and it has been greatly intensified by the long delay since the 19Gi census. To say that I am disappointed with the report now under consideration of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for Ontario would be to put it mildly. However, early in my professional career I learned that counsel achieves nothing by telling home truths to the judge. So today, with the greatest of difficulty, I resist the temptation of expressing, with the conviction which I feel, the basic home truths about those whom the parliament has made judge and jury, court of appeal and court of last resort.
One of the problems, sir, of debating redistribution is that it gives the appearance of being self-serving. I do not agree that such is the case at all. I assert that politicians in this chamber can be as objective, as impartial and as independent as any outside tribunal. Certainly my attempt tonight will be to avoid the slightest semblance of partisanship or any political self-serving and to approach the issues objectively and impartially.
Indeed, sir, I believe that if this house were to establish a subcommittee now with His Honour, the Speaker, in his capacity as the member for Stormont, in the chair, and to include the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), the hon. lady for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Wadds) and myself, we could finish redistribution of eastern Ontario ridings before midnight tonight and it would be with the unanimous approval of this house and the public and would establish the eastern Ontario ridings on a basis much fairer and more equitable to the electorate-to the electorate,
Redistribution
and I want to emphasize that-than the division proposed by the commission.
That may only indicate the extent of my personal disillusionment with the so-called independence and impartiality of the commission when the commission so obviously lacks knowledge of the geography and social and economic life of the province. If the carving up of Ontario ridings as suggested by the commission had ever been attempted by politicians under the old system a howl of gerrymandering would have gone up from coast to coast, the like of which has never been heard.
Most of my life has been spent in political organization which has taken me into every area of the province. There are few villages and townships that I have not visited and I believe I know Ontario, its geography, its economy and its social and community life. It is on the basis of a lifetime experience that I want to make submissions to the commission, with great respect to their integrity but, I say, with equal firmness.
The basic and only purpose of redistribution, Mr. Speaker, is to achieve a genuinely representative House of Commons, to permit the election of men and women to parliament who represent not merely geographic units but represent the cultural, economic and social interests of the people.
Mere arithmetical accuracy and dead mathematical uniformity does not represent a proper redistribution. Nor does it enable the people to be properly represented in this chamber. The mere drawing of lines upon a map whenever a standard number of people can be contained therein is not redistribution but is a cartographer's nightmare.
In my respectful submission, the Ontario commission made its first mistake in not accepting and using sufficiently the latitude allowed by parliament. It has attempted in the first commission redistribution too great a mathematical uniformity in the province of Ontario without using sufficiently the 25 per cent efficiency formula.
My present electoral district of Carleton is, I believe, the most populous combined rural-urban riding in all of Canada, and from my own experience I can state that an urban member of parliament can service his riding with much greater ease than a rural member. Exact numerical equality is not a genuine representation but in fact discrimination against rural areas which are thereby actually under-represented.

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
May I state to you, sir, certain principles which I submit should be applied by the commission. The first is that the alteration of electoral boundaries from one redistribution to the next should be kept at an absolute minimum. People are creatures of political and other habits, and violent upsets in electoral boundaries should be avoided where possible. Therefore, relative permanence is a proper objective and the division should be on the basis of enabling the electoral districts to accommodate expanding population with a minimum of future alteration of boundaries.
Especially is this imperative if we are to maintain proper political organizations. Regrettably no member of the Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission ever had any experience in political organization and, with respect, I venture to submit that it has ignored this important fact. This is particularly evident because of the wide departures from provincial boundaries. From Confederation until the present it has been possible in many aireas of Ontario to maintain common federal and provincial political organizations, and it will be found that in those areas political interest has been highest.
Under the proposals as they are before us a complete separation of federal and provincial organizations will be necessary, and to this there are likely to be many unsatisfactory by-products-by-prodUcts which may not contribute to our unity as a single nation. In my submission this was totally unnecessary under a proper redistribution, and the old tradition might have been maintained.
Stability of political organization is a factor which must not be overlooked if we are to preserve our parliamentary democracy. A parliamentary committee of persons who are experienced in politics and understand the nature of elections would never have permitted this to happen.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I venture to suggest that homogeneity of the ridings, culturally, socially and economically, is a vital factor in electing a genuinely representative House of Commons. The late Mackenzie King expressed this at one time as the need for "compactness".
In speaking on the second reading of the redistribution bill of 1932 this is what Mr. Mackenzie King said on November 25, 1932, as it appears in Hansard at page 1591:
There is an additional guiding principle that, so far as reasonably can be arranged, there should be an effort at compactness in the shaping of constituencies. That permits of an expression of opinion from a community that is familiar with its
[Mr. Bell (Carleton).l
own affairs, and in that way helps to give a more accurate representation of the views of the people.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
In my submission it is absolutely essential to give priority to community of interest and to balancing of population centres within the geographic unit if redistribution is to be at all fair and equitable to the electorate. Let me illustrate this by a local example. Twelve miles west of these parliament buildings are two new residential communities, slightly over a mile apart, named Kanata and Glencairn. The new Queensway to be constructed next year will make it possible to drive to either of them from these parliament buildings within 15 minutes. Both are exclusively dormitory communities-satellite towns, if you will-of this national capital, with all their ties, economic, social and cultural, here with Ottawa. By 1970 the promoters of Kanata claim it will have a population of 10,000 and Glencairn is expected to reach nearly half that figure. Yet under the proposed redistribution Kanata is to be linked with the towns of Renfrew and Perth, with which it has not the slightest affinity, whereas Glencairn, a completely similar community a mile away, is to be linked with Prescott, Cardinal and Iroquois, with which town and villages it has no association whatever. This illustrates why the members for Ontario signed the notice of objection and set forth the first reason as follows:
1.	Throughout the province of Ontario, in proposing new boundaries for electoral districts, the commission has almost completely ignored provincial and municipal electoral boundaries, social and economic ties, patterns of trade and communication, local and regional affinities as well as tradition.
Sir, I do urge the members of the Electoral Boundaries Commission earnestly to re-examine their work in the light of that objection. Without hesitation I say that the provincial redistribution, made by the same three commissioners, is much fairer, much more equitable, much more balanced.
In eastern Ontario at least, in the provincial redistribution the commission did take into account social, cultural and economic ties, patterns of trade and communication, local and regional affinities; but in the federal redistribution they have cut right across these factors.
Using the proposed electoral district of Carleton as an illustration, I say that any knowledgeable person realizes that the patterns and ties of the St. Lawrence towns and villages are east and west, with virtually no
April 28, 1966

pull toward the Ottawa river. I have met no elector of Carleton or Grenville-Dundas who does not object to this proposed riding of Grenville-Carleton, and I think they object on sound grounds.
The second objection advanced by the members from Ontario is this:
2.	The commission has proposed establishment of electoral districts having no physical, social or economic cohesion, and no unity or community of interest, thereby rendering the adequate representation of the people in parliament a virtually impossible task.
The chopping, the slicing done by the commission creates very many ridings in Ontario without cohesion, without the compactness of which Mr. Mackenzie King spoke, and thereby intensifies very greatly the problem of balanced representation by any member of parliament. Just as an illustration, the present Carleton has been sliced into five new electoral districts without any regard to the interests of the voters in the five sectors.
The third objection reads as follows:
3.	The commission has ignored the rules specified in section 13 (c) of giving attention to special geographic considerations including the sparsity, density or relative rate of growth of population of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions or the size or shape thereof.
With great respect, I submit the Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission went completely wrong in its interpretation of section 13	(c). According to the Representation
Commissioner, the commission did not examine-and I believe he asserts it was not entitled to examine-actual population growth since the census of June, 1961.
I specifically ask the commission to reconsider its position in this respect. In my view and in the opinion of a considerable number of lawyers to whom I have spoken, the commission has made a grotesque misinterpretation of the amendment made in committee of the whole on November 13, 1964. The whole purpose of the amendment was to prevent before 1971 the fantastic disparities which occurred between 1951 and 1961. The author of the amendment, Mr. Moreau, who was then the member for York-Scarborough, made it clear that he wanted to deal with factual situations subsequent to the census. I am glad to see this amendment introduced. When I spoke on this bill some months ago in

the earlier stage of its consideration I expressed the view that some account should be taken of population growth, that is the growth which had actually taken place since the census on which the redistribution was based.

There is no doubt in my mind that the absence of such a consideration at the time of the last redistribution in 1952 is one of the main reasons we have such an inequitable position at the present time as far as the suburban areas of our cities are concerned.

As indicated in the notice of objections, the electoral district I propose would be known as Carleton-Grenville-Dundas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a basic problem with the riding of Grenville-Carleton as proposed by the commission is that it could have no permanence. As I have submitted, every effort should be made to create a relative permanence from one redistribution to the next. I say to you, it is bad for parliament; it is discouraging to members and to prospective candidates; it destroys public interest; to have revolutionary changes every ten years. Every effort should be made to obviate it.
The proposed Grenville-Carleton riding, for example, has no cohesion, no mutuality of social and economic interest between the St. Lawrence front and the Ottawa valley area. On the St. Lawrence, the patterns of trade run east and west, not north and south. This redistribution runs directly counter to all historical patterns.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
I have not dealt with the redistribution of the Ottawa ridings because frankly it is beyond me, as one individual, to complete the necessary research. To prepare statistics for the Ottawa ridings such as I have given the commission, and the summary of which are placed on the record, for Grenville-Carleton would take many days of research in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and in the City of Ottawa assessment department. To do this is the responsibility of the commission staff.
These facts only I mention. In my opinion, the proposed Ottawa-Carleton riding should not cross the Rideau river to include Carleton Heights and Courtland Park, torn from the old Carleton riding. These areas simply have no mutuality of interest with the east bank of the Rideau and will turn out to be political orphans. Properly these communities belong with Nepean.
The figures for the proposed Ottawa Centre take no account of the great loss in population in that electoral district due to the expropriation and razing of LeBreton Flats and part of the Preston street area. In the proposed Ottawa West, no account is taken of the development of some of the largest apartment buildings in Canada, with many thousands of new residents. To equalize the population of Ottawa Centre and Ottawa West, certainly it is not necessary to carry the boundary of Ottawa West eastward as far as Bayswater avenue.

These are matters which I submit the commission has an obligation to re-examine and to report in detail.
Sir, I had the privilege of filing certain objections in relation to the proposed electoral districts of Etobicoke and York West and in metropolitan Toronto generally and to the readjustments in northern Ontario. Other members will be speaking on these subjects. I merely wish to say to the commission that these representations which I filed were based on serious representations made to me by political organizations in these areas, and I hope that the commissioners will give them their earnest consideration.
In conclusion, sir, I hope that the members of the commission will take very seriously the views which have been and will be expressed in this debate. They should know that the great majority of Ontario members of all parties are gravely dissatisfied with the work of the commission. These representations which we are making this evening are not mere politicians' gripes. They are an honest expression of sincere opinions of the people who do know Ontario best, who know its geography, its cultural and social affinities, its economic regions, its trade and communication patterns. It is because we, the members from Ontario, do know our Ontario that we are here representing the people in Ontario in this chamber. I say that our views and opinions publicly expressed in this chamber are entitled to respect and to sincere consideration by the commission to whom we have abdicated this vital function. Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to commend the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) for the excellent general presentation he has made in relation to the over-all problems of this redistribution. Therefore I propose to speak only of my own area.
It has been my privilege and honour to represent the good riding of Grey North since 1957. This riding embraces an area that has been in the same unit since confederation, a riding that became prominent in the famous by-election of 1945, the results of which were headline news across this nation. I might also say that I have had 14 predecessors since the birth of Canada. Needless to say, each has made a worthy contribution and I pay tribute to them.
I object to the boundaries as set up for the new proposed riding of Grey Simcoe because of the complete disregard for the social, cultural and economic interests of the municipalities that are grouped together. For instance, the townships of Flos and Tiny on the east are closely linked with Penetang and Midland, and they should remain in the same riding as these two towns because they have little in common with Owen Sound on the west. On the other hand, Keppel, Sarawak and Derby townships have everything in common with Owen Sound. In fact, hundreds of people from these townships work in that city; yet the new boundary eliminates these municipalities from that city in their midst and from the riding.
The geographical aspects have certainly been ignored, and from this point of view it would be virtually impossible to have unity or community of interest.
Another important factor that must be considered and which, of course, has developed since the census was taken is the designation of the Georgian bay area. Several new, large factories will be in production this year and others are under construction, so that an immediate population growth is assured. As further evidence of the impending development, which will certainly result in increased population, I would like to read an excerpt from an article in yesterday's Owen Sound Sun-Times which came to my hand today. The heading is "Many industries showing interest in Owen Sound", and the article goes on:
Negotiations are proceeding with a dozen or more industrial prospects for Owen Sound. Some appear

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
likely to result in plants being located here; others are more remote. Such was the report of industrial commissioner R. C. Taylor to members of Owen Sound civic development committee Tuesday evening.
We in Grey North concur in the riding as set up under provincial redistribution where some recognition was given to several significant features that have apparently been overlooked by the federal planners. I am reluctant to see any severance take place, but I do appreciate the fact that constituencies will necessarily have to be adjusted to bring some semblance of uniformity to the size of the ridings in respect of population. However, Mr. Speaker, there are other important factors which should not be overlooked.
In an area such as I represent, I feel a riding should be built around a traditional trading centre. A city or town, to enjoy this popularity, should be of easy access to the surrounding communities. It would have most of the services that attract people, such as good medical and dental facilities, adequate shopping centres, market accommodation, educational institutions, places of entertainment and culture. In fact, it would be a place where people have traditionally congregated for various reasons over the years.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I propose the peninsula area, with Owen Sound as the focal point of the new riding, the southern boundary to begin at Lake Huron on the west, follow the southern boundary of Saugeen, Elderslie, Sullivan, Holland, Euphrasia and Collingwood townships, and then north to Georgian Bay. The population of this compact area would be within a few hundreds in population of the ill-considered, incoherent proposition for the new riding of Grey-Simcoe.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote an excerpt from a radio broadcast editorial of June 21, 1965, emanating from the only station in our immediate area, CFOS:
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
The commission's report, made public earlier this week, recommends that parts of Grey county be associated with parts of Simcoe county to form a new federal electoral district to be called Grey-Simcoe. We also are aware that it will not be possible to make boundary decisions which will please everyone. But, at the same time, we suggest further consideration be given to the recommended arrangements for this part of the province. Although we have the highest regard for the people of Simcoe county, we think a combination of Grey and Bruce counties would make a more suitable community. A close association between the people of Grey and Bruce counties has been developed over a span of many years.

We believe this association between the people of Grey and Bruce counties is an excellent foundation for the marriage of the two counties for the purposes of representation in both the federal and provincial governments. If a combination of the two counties is regarded by the commission as too large to be properly represented by one member, we suggest that the southern townships in Grey county could be associated with Wellington county and in the case of Bruce, the southern townships could be associated with Huron county.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is abundantly clear to the interested people in our area that adjustments to the proposed plan will necessarily have to be made to save what now appears to be almost a ridiculous situation. Indeed, if the new federal lines are approved for Grey-Simcoe, it will be extremely awkward for any elected representative to serve adequately.
One can only trust that the wisdom which prevailed in the ultimate policies followed by Ontario officials in setting out the perimeter lines will to some extent, form the guide lines which federal authorities will use to establish the final pattern.

[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

This means that the new constituency which I or someone else will be representing in this house would extend to the Hamilton city limits. There have been widespread objections in the press and elsewhere from the residents of Ancaster township to the effect that never in history have they had anything in common, any common association, with the people of Brantford. This is regrettable as far as I am concerned. I love my city and I want to say right now that I would love to represent the township of Ancaster in this House of Commons, a beautiful township if there ever was one. I want to make it abundantly clear that I have no political reason for stating this. But

I believed the objections of the people as placed before the commission should have been taken into consideration. Certainly the commission did take account of some of the objections filed. The commission did make changes after hearing from numerous bodies whose representatives appeared before it after its findings had been made public.
Ancaster includes not only the township but a great village which is sometimes called the dormitory village of the city of Hamilton. A more historic or beautiful village cannot be found in the province. But the people of this area go to Hamilton for all their shopping. They go there to conduct all their business. They go there to attend the sessions of the courts as well as for every matter affecting their daily lives. They do not like being incorporated in the new proposed riding of Brant. They do not have a common background with Brant economically or politically-1 do not know about culturally. Certainly they have always looked to Hamilton as the centre of their activities
I turn, now, to the little township of Oakland. Having added the township of Ancaster to the constituency I represent, the commission took away a very small township, the township of Oakland. Oakland is one of the smallest townships, if not the smallest, in the province of Onatrio. The people of Oakland were much incensed about this action on the part of the commission-so much so that they circulated a petition and filed it with the Speaker of the House of Commons. It is here for everyone to see.
There are just over 700 electors in the township and more than 500 of them signed this petition to the Speaker of the House of Commons saying they did not want to be taken from the proposed constituency of Brant and put into the new constituency of Oxford. This little township forms a wedge, a wedge which is not without historical significance. I feel that if nothing else is done the wishes of the population of Oakland should be respected. As far as the constituency is concerned, it does not make much difference where the 700 people vote but it does make a great deal of difference to the residents. I am informed that nearly 100 per cent of the electorate would have signed the petition but it was circulated in a hurry so as to get it before the house quickly and it did not reach everyone. Still, more than 75 per cent of the people in Oakland did sign it. In these circumstances, as the member of parliament representing this area at the moment, I feel it

is only my duty to make whatever representations I can on behalf of these people.
The inhabitants of Oakland reside within six miles of the centre of Brantford. They go to Brantford for all their business. They go into Brantford for meetings-public meetings and meetings of organized groups. They take part in the affairs of Brant county. They go into the courthouse of Brant county-the county courthouse is situated in the middle of the city of Brantford. Now they have to look to the city of Woodstock and I am told by these people that they do not go to Woodstock for anything. They are asked to select a member of parliament to represent them in the House of Commons from an area dominated largely by the great county of Oxford. They feel they will in some way be cast out-that they will no longer enjoy the kind of representation they have had in this house in the past.
I wish to say a word, now, about one other township, a much larger township with over 2,700 qualified electors, which under this redistribution has also been assigned to Oxford. I am speaking of Burford, and the same feeling exists in Burford as exists in Oakland. These people go to Brantford for everything connected with their business. Ever since 1852 when Brant county was set up, a little later than the other counties, the residents of Burford have gone to Brantford on all their business.
Brant county does seem to form a cohesive unit, I must say. The people of Burford feel that separated from the county with which they have always been associated they are not likely to be represented as effectively, as a unit, as they have in the past. I should like the commissioners to take account of this feeling and act accordingly. 1 believe they will do so because this commission has, on the whole, done a very good job considering the task placed before it. Some of these decisions do affect my constituents.
I have no quarrel with the name which has been selected-the name "Brant". In the absence of that name even the people who at the present time compose the electors of my constituency would feel they had been cut off completely. They feel at home with the great name of Brant, so I shall not complain about that decision. I am not complaining about everything the commission has done. I want to commend the commissioners on having put into my present constituency the township of South Dumfries, a great township. The residents come to Brantford for everything. This
April 28, 1966

brought into the new riding the town of Paris, a beautiful town, and this too was a commendable decision.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
This is the way it had been in the first proposed division. In their first proposed setup of the new constituency the commission had put Paris in Wellington county to be represented in this house. It has been changed. This new change is far better for the people of Paris and far better for the people of South Dumfries. That was done because those people attended before the commission and were able to have the change made, so that they will come in the new riding of Brant where they should be and where they might be expected to be.
I am only going to say in review, Mr. Speaker, that I feel the commission should pay special attention to the four points I have mentioned. I believe on reconsideration and upon looking at the work the commission did in revamping the provincial boundaries, they will see that it is probably better to leave in the new riding of Brant those units which always have been around, and have revolved around, the centre of the city of Brantford over the years. If Ancaster township were taken off and Burford and Oakland put back on along with South Dumfries, as the commission has rightly done, I believe that would be a good constituency, together with Onondaga.
If it cannot be worked out in any other way by the commission and if Ancaster cannot be put any other place, I will be glad to accept it, but I do not want to see Burford and Oakland taken off. In the new proposed constituency I would have the largest constituency in the province of Ontario; I do not object to that. I would be sort of proud to think I represented so many people, provided I was elected.
I feel I have put on record my few objections and I would seriously like to have the commission consider them very carefully, in the hope that perhaps a better drafting can be made of a new constituency there-because there has to be one-we all know that. I should like to put on record one other little point. It has been suggested to me and also suggested unofficially recently to members of the commission that Ancaster township be split at the Shaver's side road, to which I have no objection, and that the village of
Redistribution
Ancaster and that part which lies immediately beside the city of Hamilton be incorporated into one of the ridings in Wentworth. Then the rest could quite readily be assimilated into Brant county. But that is a matter I would leave to the discretion of the commission in its wisdom.
I have given my opinion in respect of these proposed changes. I have been fair, I hope, and I wish to make one thing clear: there are no politics whatsoever involved in the remarks I have made. It does not make any difference to me. I am only too glad to represent that whole new area; but it is the people themselves who are dissatisfied, and I think their feelings should be brought forward. Personally it makes no difference to me. The Brantford Expositor had an editorial criticizing all the members who wanted these changes made and said that an independent commission had given its views, and that now they wanted to bring it back into politics. I do not want it brought back into politics. I want a fair, impartial finding made, and I believe the commission will do that, upon considering all the facts and circumstances.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for me to ascertain whether the applause is approbation for my standing to participate in the speeches or because my constituency is disappearing. Unlike the previous speaker, who says he does not mind the great area being added to his constituency, I am one of those who will have nothing left to represent as such.
Mr. Speaker, I think the way we are proceeding now is a wise one, provided the commissioners will pay attention to the words spoken by the members in this house. The reason I bring this forward is simply this, that I do not believe we can justifiably deal with the implications of redistribution without considering the political aspirations and the other points which have been raised in this regard. Therefore, as some hon. members have mentioned, to keep it on an independent basis and in the hands of an independent commission outside the House of Commons, I think it would be only fair that the representations being put forward here on behalf of the different constituencies and provinces be given some attention, so that in the final analysis all the words spoken here in this unusual type of debate would not be redundant.

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
I would hope that the members of the commissions have sufficient cognizance of the political abilities of the people in the House of Commons to give a fair and sympathetic hearing to the changes which have been requested, and act accordingly. To begin with, let me refer back to a few of the hopes that were set forth at the time the measure was introduced in the House of Commons. I wish to refer to the words of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who, in speaking on March 10 had this do say, as reported at page 739 of Hansard:
The second principle was that in doing this we should not abdicate the final responsibility which is imposed upon this parliament, and we would have to find some means of making sure that we did not just turn this matter over to a commission without any final power in parliament at least to object if any palpable and obvious errors seemed by the majority to have been made.
This is in support of my opening remarks, and again I only make the plea that the commissioners heed the words of those who have spoken. At a later time he went on to say:
We will welcome improvements from any quarter of the house.
This is at page 743 of Hansard. He was quoting at that time from a previous Hansard. I will refer to another objective:
That such commission in so doing shall consider the distribution of population according to the then latest census of Canada and the public interest and convenience-
I shall have some remarks on that in a few moments.
-and shall particularly have regard so far as practicable to the boundaries of the counties, municipalities and cities.
I think it has been pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) that in many cases this has not been given proper attention. I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the interests of the public and their convenience, as has been pointed out in my specific petition, has not been given proper consideration. At a previous time in this debate Mr. Moreau, the former member for York-Scarborough was very critical of a contribution I made and referred to my remarks as being associated with rural tyranny so far as constituencies such as his are concerned.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I want it very clearly understood that I do not object to the commission or to redistribution. I do not object to what has happened to my riding. I do object, however, to the method

used by the commission as indicated by the proposed map of constituencies in southern Ontario. I must add at this point that my objections are based on an interest for the people of Ontario whom I represent. First, they have not been properly served. Second, the centres of population and natural lines of communication have been disregarded. Third, traditional boundaries have been ignored. Fourth, in consideration of the counties of Grey and Bruce, plus some adjacent territory, they might have been divided into two contiguous constituencies, having similar interests. Therefore, the lines have been improperly drawn. Fifth, there is little or no similarity between the new boundaries and the boundaries being considered for provincial redistribution.
Mr. Speaker, I have been supported in these objections by the words of one of the ministers who spoke prior to the printing of these principal objections. If my words at this time are true, it would seem to me that the commission has a serious responsibility to take another look at the proposed map. None of us has any right to make amendments or do anything but make suggestions. We must therefore depend upon the integrity of the commissioners to deal with the situation accordingly.
The speaker preceding me made some reference to the city of Paris. I have in my hands a copy of The Ayr News dated Thursday, June 24, 1965 in which there is a prediction of what they expect will happen in Paris. Things apparently turned out differently. For the sake of the people of that area I hope things worked out well, because it states here that the people of this particular area do not like to be divided.
It seems, according to some comments that have been made today, that we have become too sophisticated to use words like "gerrymandering" or "hiving". In order to describe what has happened we use the word "redistribution". Perhaps that is an appropriate way of describing the system or method used to eliminate the riding I have the honour to represent. I have often wondered, since the proposed maps were produced, whether it is a mere coincidence that my colleague, the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble) and my colleague, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Loney) and myself happen to find ourselves now in one proposed new constituency. It seems to me that the line is very narrow in respect of two cases for anyone to believe that this is a matter of coincidence.
April 28. 1966

My colleague, the hon. member for Grey North and myself have done a substantial amount of research regarding the constituencies we now represent and which are about to disappear, unless further consideration is given to the proposed changes. When the preliminary maps were drawn the commissioner invited me to view them. That map was exactly as the map now before us. With my knowledge of the political and constituency structure of Ontario I thought the work regarding the southern part of the province was reasonable.
It was my belief then that the lines, running north and south in the heavily populated areas, created the kind of division which would allow necessary flexibility for the future, in view of expanding population. I suggested to the commissioner at that time that the lines in the northern part of southern Ontario should run east and west, and I impressed upon him my reasons for that suggestion. Apparently my words had no effect because the map now before us is exactly the same as the preliminary one I had the opportunity of seeing.
At the present time the population in my constituency is 36,883. This is quite low, but there are constituencies with smaller populations. I pointed out my political philosophic thinking to the commissioner, and in this regard I should like to agree with the remarks of the preceding speaker when he said that he was speaking in the interests of the people of this area. I have always conducted my political life on that basis and will continue to do so in the future.
I suggest that the new lines for my riding and the riding of Grey North, as well as the ridings south and east of this area, be drawn in an east-west direction. This would create a tremendous advantage and provide flexibility for future expansion. By doing so we would create a constituency with a population of 66,967 with a division approximately midway in the counties of Grey and Bruce in an east-west direction. This would include very few townships, towns and villages which are not now included but it would create two constituencies exactly similar, in that they have the same type of people, growth and prospects.
As the hon. member for Grey North pointed out, the proposed constituency would have two centres of population at opposite ends, made up of people with varying interests. The flow of the people in both communities would cross two constituencies, making it
Redistribution
very difficult for any representative to do a good job.
In my own constituency one centre of the population is in the southeast corner. Obviously the flow of these people is toward or into the city of Owen Sound. At this particular time a provincial redistribution map is drawn in such a way that it takes this fact into account. That is not so regarding the proposed lines for the federal constituency.
I think the proposed map is unfair in another respect. Since this government has taken office many things have been inequitable. The hon. member for Grey North found it possible to thank the government for establishing part of his constituency as a designated area. Everyone understood that this was the Georgian bay economic area. I should point out that it is the southern area of the constituency that is more in need, but that that area has been left out of the designated area. This kind of thing will happen more often and result in more confusion, particularly if the government is not aware of the existing boundaries.
Again let me emphasize that I am not objecting in any way because a member will have to serve a larger area with a greater population; but let me suggest that members representing urban ridings find their jobs much easier than those representing rural ridings, because government offices and services are always available to them, whereas they are not as assessible in rural areas. A member representing a rural area must perform a greater degree of personal service for his constituents than does a member representing an urban riding. This has been verified by the remarks of hon. members on both sides of the house.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I say that the lines as now drawn will make it very, very difficult for rural members to carry out their responsibilities and are not at all consistent with the best interests of the people. If the best interests of the people had been considered I believe that the lines for the northern, heavily populated areas of southern Ontario would have run east and west, as I have suggested, rather than being in the jumbled pattern that is now before us. I have only to think of the constituency of my hon. friend from Cochrane to realize what a terrible mess can be made in this regard and how completely unreasonable the boundaries of one riding can be. I do not even have to refer to my own constituency to prove this point.

April 28. 1966
Redistribution
Reference has been made to the words of wisdom contained in the brief presented by Mr. Inrig to the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Ontario. I believe that parts of this brief should be placed on the record of the house for the information of hon. members and the commission, who will then have it before them for their consideration of the suggestions placed before the house. Mr. George F. W. Inrig of Lindsay, Ontario, deserves commendation for the amount of work and effort he put into this brief, which contains many valuable suggestions which I believe could be used by the commission in its subsequent days of consideration. The brief says in part:
The organization of political parties and the participation of the political party in the democratic process requires a consistent geographical unit within which to function.
This is one of my basic arguments against what has been done with the counties of Grey and Bruce. The brief continues:
The alteration of electoral district boundaries should be kept at a minimum.
Not only have they not been kept at a minimum but they have been changed so as to cause confusion for political organization, regardless of the party to which a member belongs. The brief then says:
It is, therefore, desirable that, whenever possible, the alteration of electoral district boundaries should be made only after taking into consideration the community of interest of the residents and the location of the population centres within the geographical unit-
Again, Mr. Speaker, this is the type of objection I have taken and I do not believe the commissioners applied this thinking when considering southwestern Ontario. Mr. Inrig goes on to say:
Regardless of population, the urban representative can service his constituency with greater ease than the rural representative who must cover wide territories. This is not equality of representation.
Again this is in support of my statement with regard to government services, which are found in urban areas and certainly not in rural areas where the member must himself carry on these services. The brief also states:
Redistribution, as it has been proposed by this commission, should it occur every 10 years, would mean the end of political organization in this province.
With the population as it is in Canada today, and with the reasonable understanding that I think all of us have, namely that what Canada needs more than anything else is people, I believe that if we have the ability to

organize, assimilate, absorb people and create jobs quickly enough, it would not be impossible for us soon to absorb 20 million or 30 million people for the benefit of our economic future. However, I believe that the commission has not been looking into the future. Then the brief says:
It is not suggested that this redistribution is not necessary, but it is submitted that redistribution of this magnitude occurring every 10 years would be a serious detriment to political organization.
I believe a great many of us would be prepared to agree with that statement. As I said, this is a valuable brief and one which I think agrees with the thinking of most members. I am glad to be able to place these remarks on the record for the consideration of the commission.
On an earlier occasion when I participated in the debate on this matter I was widely criticized by the press. I have here a letter to the Globe and Mail criticizing me for making these remarks because I represent in parliament such a small number of people. As I have said, other constituencies are smaller than mine. I was also criticized for wailing about gerrymandering. I do not think I used the word "gerrymander" at that time but, as I said earlier, I sometimes wonder whether it was a coincidence that this situation has developed. In the lifetime of parliament this situation does not, of course, happen very often. Sometimes I think that had my predecessor still been in office, some other means would possibly have been found to deal with this situation.
We do not put these matters before the commission simply for the sake of argument. My colleague from Grey North used the editorial comment of radio station CFOS to bear out his point. I agree completely with him. Apparently this was the consensus at the time and remains so today. I believe the lines on this map have been poorly drawn with regard to southwestern Ontario. Consideration should be given to their being changed in order that in the future the best type of service may be obtained for constituents by members elected to the house. This service cannot be provided with the boundaries drawn as they are in this map, in which you have people from the tip of the Bruce peninsula coming down to the southeast corner of Grey county. From the central, northern part of Grey county the lines run down almost into the city of Waterloo. There is no community of interest whatsoever there. There is no community of interest on the
April 28, 1966

other side. There is no community of interest for the people in the riding of my colleague from Grey North. The suggestions I have placed on record will make no difference to me politically, as I explained to the commissioner, but surely the advice and suggestions of members of this house deserve consideration by the commission, because they are fair, sensible and equitable.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak very briefly on this matter as it affects Ontario ridings. My remarks will be similar to those of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), because I do not wish to go into detail and shall make just two general points. My remarks will have reference to the twin counties of Waterloo North and Waterloo South.
A name has been mentioned in the house this evening, that of one of our great prime ministers, and I would remind hon. members that the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King was born in the riding of Waterloo North and first served as a member of that riding.
The point I wish to make was mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). I have no objection to the idea of an independent commission dealing with the question of redistribution, provided that the proper criteria were used by them and arbitrary decisions were not made. The hon. member for Carleton mentioned population growth. I think we all know of the tremendous growth of our urban areas. The growth of population in the two cities in my riding is 4 per cent annually, and their boundaries are not fixed. As the commissioners well know, but for the benefit of hon. members of the house, I would point out that under redistribution the two ridings of Waterloo North and Waterloo South are joined together. Both are in what I consider to be one of the finest counties of Ontario, but the people of the north have a little different background from the people of the south.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Out of the centre of this combination is formed the new urban riding of the city of Kitchener, what I call the hole in the doughnut. With all respect to independent commissions, I may say that since I have been in this place I have found it is impossible to talk to an independent commission. I am wondering whether, in determining this new configuration, the growth potential of this urban municipality was taken into consideration. As I am very well aware, and as our rural neighbours are aware, it is possible that
Redistribution
within a few years the city of Kitchener will reach out to the boundaries of the county and the new riding of Waterloo will be cut in half.
When the riding of Waterloo South was joined with Waterloo North to form the new riding of Waterloo, the town of Elmira and a rural area which for years has been associated economically and socially with the twin cities of Kitchener and Waterloo were cut off. I believe that this area will be joined to the riding to the north. In so far as an independent commission is concerned, I can say that if this redistribution had been in the hands of parliamentary committee many members could give a very sympathetic hearing to these many problems. If a job has to be done, then you certainly have to take the ultimate objective into consideration and some things have to be changed.
The other point I wish to make is one that probably affects other Ontario ridings. The federal redistribution took place concurrently with provincial redistribution. I feel that there might have been closer liaison and some different decisions made. When the two ridings of Waterloo were changed to form two new ridings in the area, we found that we had four new ridings, two provincial and two federal. This in itself, causes more confusion. We now have four organizations for the various political parties. Again I say that this job could have been done a little better. I certainly hope that in registering my objection, not a strong objection, the commission will take these matters into consideration.
Mr. W. C. Scott (Victoria (Ont.)h At this point, Mr. Speaker, I do not complain about my riding being too small, but rather I complain about its being too large under the proposed redistribution. I feel that in a democratic state the role of a political party is in the selection, promotion and election of candidates for public office; in assisting the elected representatives in the solicitation, assessment and qualification of opinion and in the discrimination of policy. It is through the means of the political party that peaceful change in government can occur.
In order to be effective, political parties must be highly organized. They cannot operate as loosely knit associations but must be united, disciplined organizations reaching every segment of the community and representing the main interests of society. The establishment of poll, ward and township organizations is tempered, if not destroyed, by the continuous alteration of electoral

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
boundaries. Although it may be true that permanent establishment of electoral boundaries is not possible, alterations should be kept to a minimum.
One factor in political organizations is that the participation of the citizen in political activities is affected by the interest of the individual in and the accessibility of the individual to the major population centre of the geographical unit. In other words, a citizen will be a participant in political organization if he resides within the sphere of the community of interest of the political unit. It is therefore desirable that wherever possible the alteration of electoral district boundaries should be made only after taking into consideration the community of interest of the residents and the location of the population centres within the geographical unit. This is necessary if an effort is to be made to encourage citizens to become involved in political activity.
It is submitted that it is the duty of a citizen in a democratic state to become involved in politics because it is only through an active, interested, informed participating electorate that democratic government can succeed. The elected representative, whether he be a member of the House of Commons or a member of a provincial legislature, not only represents people as individuals within his electoral district but he also represents the geographical unit, the social, cultural, economic and many other interests within his electoral district. It is submitted that it is as important that the elected representative be physically able to represent his geographical unit, as it is that the people within the various geographical units have numerically equal representation.
Although those citizens residing within the heavily populated areas of our nation demand redistribution to establish numerically equal representation, the citizens residing in the less densely populated areas are entitled also to equal representation. We do not mean, in this context, numerical equality but rather equality of service which is dependant upon the ease and accessibility with which the elected representative can communicate with his electorate. The urban resident may believe he is under-represented because there is a greater population in the urban constituency than in the rural constituency. The rural resident may believe he is under-represented because the urban constituency is composed

of a dozen city blocks, while the rural constituency is composed of 50 or more townships. Regardless of population, the urban representative can service his constituency with greater ease than the rural representative who must cover wide territories. This is not equality of representation.
It is, therefore, desirable that in establishing the electoral district boundaries, not only should numerical factors be taken into consideration, but geographical factors must be considered to enable the elected representative effectively to represent his constituency and to encourage the citizens to become involved in political activity.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Directing attention to the areas affected by the proposed electoral district of Victoria-Haliburton, it will be seen that the counties of Ontario, Victoria, Haliburton, Peterborough, Hastings, Renfrew and Nipissing are involved. The proposal of the commission is to establish the riding of Victoria-Haliburton, comprising the county of Victoria, the provincial county of Haliburton, three townships from the county of Ontario, eight townships from the county of Peterborough, six townships from the county of Hastings, five townships from the county of Nipissing and three townships from the county of Renfrew.
This proposal removes the township of Brock from the existing electoral district of Victoria and adds 22 new townships to the existing riding. The proposed riding will consist of 60 townships, the town of Lindsay, the villages of Havelock, Fenelon Falls, Bob-caygeon, Beaverton, Woodville, Minden, Haliburton, Omemee, Barrys Bay, and many other smaller hamlets. It can be said that the population centres of the proposed riding will be centred around Lindsay, Havelock and Barrys Bay.
The township of Brock is within the sphere of the community of interest formed by the four northern townships of the county of Ontario, namely Rama, Mara, Thora and Brock. These four townships have been politically connected for a long time with the present electoral district of Victoria. I find that the residents of Brock township have strong social and economic ties with the Lindsay area as well as with the people in the three adjoining townships to the north. Their political affiliations have been for a long time very closely connected with the existing Victoria riding. If they are forced to change their political organization, the result
April 28, 1966

will be that the citizens of the township of Brock will have little interest in participating in political activities. Therefore I suggest that the township of Brock be included in the proposed riding of Victoria-Haliburton.
The proposed riding of Victoria-Haliburton is geographically too large, although it is not numerically large. The electors of this area would be under-represented if one member of parliament were expected to cover this territory. It is acknowledged that there are ridings to the north of this riding which may be geographically larger, but the problem of representing these ridings is not as great, as the population is centred along waterways and rail lines. In the proposed riding of Victoria-Haliburton three major population centres exist, namely Lindsay, which will be the political centre of the riding, Havelock and Barrys Bay. As well, there are other population centres such as Beaverton and Haliburton.
Although the major population centre of the riding, Lindsay, is situated in the southwestern corner of the proposed riding, Barrys Bay is situated in the northeastern corner of the new riding and lies some 100 miles as the crow flies from Lindsay. By road the distance is approximately 140 miles.
A former representative of Victoria riding, Sir Sam Hughes, is reported to have told reporters that if he drove as far south from Lindsay as it was necessary for him to drive north to reach the farthest extent of his riding, he would end up in New York state. The representative of the new riding of Victoria-Halliburton could claim to end up in Lake Erie, if not in Ohio, should he drive as far southwesterly from Lindsay as it will be necessary for him to drive northeasterly to reach the farthest extent of his new riding.
The village of Barrys Bay, and the three townships taken from the county of Renfrew, Burns, Jones and Sherwood, as well as the five townships of the county of Nipissing, that is, Airy, Murchison, Dickens, Sabine and Lyell, have no community of interest with Lindsay nor with the other areas of the Pembroke-Renfrew community. The road system leads to Pembroke and Renfrew. To associate with the other areas of Victoria-Haliburton, the residents of this area would have to pass through either the new riding of Hastings or through the new riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka.
There is absolutely no connection, community of interest, or common bond between this northeastern area and the rest of the
Redistribution
proposed riding of Victoria-Haliburton. It is submitted that this area should be united with the ridings to the north or to the east.
By adding the township of Brock, whose political ties have been with the people of Victoria-Haliburton riding, to the proposed riding of Victoria-Haliburton would more than compensate for the population loss of the eight northeastern townships, whose political affiliations have never been with the Victoria-Haliburton constituency.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. J. P. Cameron (High Park):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in this debate for a short period of time. My argument is much narrower than that advanced by other hon. members. I have one contention only which I want to make and to pass through you, Mr. Speaker, back to the commissioners. It is a submission which I think they will entertain and deal with in a kindly manner.
My representation is for the retention of the name of High Park for that substantial part of the riding which has been taken into the new riding of Humber Valley. In this connection may I say that High Park was created a riding in 1924. Since that time there have been 13 general elections, and I have been involved in every one of them, nine times as a candidate and at other times as official agent, returning officer, and so forth. I have also lived in the riding for the better part of my life, so that you can see, Mr. Speaker, it really does mean something to me personally to see the name of High Park retained.
Apropos of that, may I place on the record a representation which I received from a number of persons in the present riding of High Park. It reads as follows:
At a duly constituted meeting ol the special committee to look into the proposed redistribu-ion of the boundaries of the federal riding of High Park which took place on February 23, 1966; and after a thorough discussion re same it was unanimously resolved;
Whereas the new redistribution of federal ridings has proposed to incorporate certain sections of the High Park federal riding into the ridings of Davenport, Parkdale and Humber Valley, and thereby eradicating the present riding of High Park;
May I observe, in passing, that I do not agree with what was said by my hon. friend from Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), because I will still be living in the riding, and if at that particular time I do have any political aspirations I am sure I can find a very comfortable home in any one of the three parts into which my riding has been divided. I am sure

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
the same thing will apply to the hon. member tor Grey-Bruce.
After that interpolation may I resume my reading of this resolution.
And whereas our association deems it in the best interest of the residents in this area to retain the symbolic name of High Park which includes in this area High Park, being synonymous with open spaces for leisure, flowers and gardens, etc., which has greatly enhanced the character and tranquil beauty of our city of Toronto.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
And whereas since the re-distribution was based on 1961 population figures it is now obvious due to high rise developments in the High Park area that there shall be a much greater concentrated population therein than was initially anticipated.
And whereas for the reasons above stated the provincial committee on redistribution has found it advisable to retain most of the present provincial boundaries of High Park.
And whereas a greater portion of Humber Valley comprises the old riding of High Park; our committee strongly recommends that the name of High Park be retained as a federal riding constituency for the proposed riding redistribution.
May I say, as a contestant in nine elections, as one who has practised law in that riding for many years, and as one who is very well acquainted with the population of the riding, that I am sure I speak on behalf of all persons in the riding when I say that they want to retain the name of High Park.
At the present time the riding consists of 160 polls. Up until the last election it had 162 polls. Owing to the fact that the east-west subway cut through that riding, there was a considerable diminution of homes, and the returning officer in her wisdom reduced the number of polls.
There are 23 pools in Parkdale which belonged to the riding and which quite legitimately have been added to what is now called the riding of High Park and which has been renamed by the commission "Parkdale".
Fifty eight polls have gone into the riding of Davenport, which is proper and legitimate. The name "Davenport" is the proper name for that riding. I say that because Parkdale was a small community which was built up on the outskirts of York, and then Toronto, and Davenport was another small community which was built up on the outskirts of Toronto, and became part of Toronto but retained that cohesive quality of having been a former municipality.
I had an opportunity of writing to the commission when the first report was filed. I appreciated the position of my hon. friend from Parkdale when he found that his riding

was called "High Park". The commission retained the name in that respect.
I was equally surprised when I found what is now Davenport had been called Parkdale, because there was no historic association between Parkdale and Davenport any more than there was between Parkdale and High Park. High park, and I am now speaking of the park, was incorporated in High Park riding during the time of its inception. No harm will be done if it is taken back. It has been put into Parkdale. I am going to suggest to the commission that it be taken back into the riding which I think they should call High Park. There are approximately three voters in that particular park.
Then, the commissioners in their wisdom have included eight polling subdivisions in an area encompassed by a line running westerly along Bloor street south to Humberside avenue and over to Quebec avenue. The commissioners will know what I mean when they refer to their maps.
I am suggesting that they exchange those eight polling subdivisions and take in lieu several polling subdivisions, which would give them a line on Bloor street to the east and west running along the line of the Canadian Pacific tracks and lying east of Pacific avenue. In that way they would be able to retain the division of the population, and the basic numbers that they have arrived at. That appears to be very fair and very reasonable.
High park itself is a great national park, fully the equal of Stanley park in British Columbia, and is one of the great parks in Canada and one of the breathing spots of the citizens of Toronto. To lose such a symbolic name now appears to me to be tragic.
As I mentioned earlier, I had the opportunity of appearing before the commission. I had written to them on behalf of my hon. friend, the member for Parkdale (Mr. Hai-dasz), suggesting that the name of "High Park" was inappropriate for that riding. I had also written to the commission about the renaming of Davenport as "Parkdale". Unfortunately I made no representations myself at that time about the name of High Park, intending to appear before the commission to express my views. On September 30 I found myself unavoidably otherwise engaged and therefore I was unable to be present. You can imagine my surprise, Mr. Speaker, when I got the final report and found that the name "High Park" had disappeared completely from the map.
April 28, 1966

While the name "Humber River" is a very important and a very historic name, because the Humber river was the gateway to Georgian bay in the north, the gateway of the Huron Indians, the pathway followed by Brule, Champlain and others, and is a name that I honour, I am sure that the people who live in the area, and I expect the commissioners are not unmindful of this, would not object to the name of their riding being changed to "High Park-Humber Valley". You will notice that I put High Park first. The name should be High Park. If the people living along the river or near it wish to bring in Humber Valley, we shall be glad and happy to have that added to our name.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my representation. My riding, like Gaul, has been divided into three parts. Having been associated with it in 13 elections I have established many contacts and I have a great many friends. No matter what you do there is bound to be a separation of the community of interest which has been developed over 42 years. But whatever the riding is, the riding of High Park has within its boundaries some of the finest citizens of Canada.
So far as any political aspirations of mine in the future are concerned, I can say that any one of these ridings would be a place I should be honoured to represent. At the present time I want to represent to the best of my ability the people of High Park riding, whom I regard as being among the finest citizens of the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most hon. members of this house, I rise in this debate to speak with mixed feelings. As other hon. members who have mentioned this, I agree that this debate should be as non-political as possible, but only non-political to the extent that political advantage should not be taken of geographic rearranging for specific political purposes. I do think that it should be political, however, for the purpose of maintaining political activity and political enthusiasm in certain parts of the country.
[DOT] (8:50 n.m.)
We in Grenville-Dundas have known that with redistribution there would be definite changes in the old riding as it has been constituted for many years. We knew that we had three ways to expand, being on the St. Lawrence river and bordering the United States. We knew that the expansion would go east, north, or west.
Redistribution
Our main interest and concern from the beginning was that the old riding nucleus and base would be used, if possible, for the base of expansion. We felt that the interest and activity in the political world for which Grenville-Dundas has long been famous might thereby extend into an equally enthusiastic and active, if larger, riding, whatever its geographical area might be. We recognized that it was necessary for some of the very large ridings to be made smaller because of the impossibility of properly representing so many constituents. At the same time it was apparent that smaller ridings such as Grenville-Dundas, where everyone knew everyone else, at least by family name, would have to be enlarged. We hoped that a close knowledge of and interest in the political scene would be encouraged within the larger unity. Representations have already been made to the commission regarding the division of the old established county of Dundas. The people there feel very strongly about the separation of two of its townships from two other townships.
Having looked carefully over the population figures of eastern Ontario I believe this complaint could be met if there were a slight rearrangement. It is possible that during this debate some other arrangement might be outlined and that this, too, would prove acceptable. But in looking over the population averages of the eastern Ontario ridings I find these range between roughly 55,000 and 81,-
000.	Glengarry-Prescott, Leeds, Grenville-Carleton and Stormont all have a population in the area of 60,000. If a township such as Cumberland, which is largely rural and which has a population of just over 6,000 were taken from the proposed Ottawa-Carleton riding of more than 74,000, this would still leave the mainly urban Ottawa-Carleton constituency with over 68,000, well within the general average. If Cumberland were added to Glengarry-Prescott instead of Russell and Cambridge, which together have a population slightly over 6,000, this would leave the riding of Glengarry-Prescott almost exactly as it is now, that is, around 62,000. If Russell and Cambridge townships directly adjoining Stormont county on the north were added to Stormont it would leave Stormont with about
64,000,	still within the average of the eastern Ontario units.
With Winchester remaining part of Dundas county this would still leave Grenville-Carleton with a little over 74,000, within the

April 28, 1966
Redistribution
general average of the new population figures.
In making these representations I am not speaking for myself. I am representing many people and many families who have taken part in Canadian politics for generations. They wish to be fair, and in all the conversations I have had on the subject they have expressed this wish. I believe it is fair to ask that in the course of this necessary process of redistribution Dundas county should remain unbroken in whatever unit it joins. As I have said, there may be other arrangements which would achieve this end and I am sure that with continued good will and effort there can be compromise among the various opinions expressed during this debate. I trust the commission will take into account the detailed knowledge which most members of parliament have of their ridings and of the relationships involved.
I am sure the interests of Dundas county would be better served if the old Grenville-Dundas riding were used as a basis for future expansion. In this way the splendid and active interest which the area has always taken in politics will continue. It would seem to me that when minor changes can be made on the grounds of a homogeneity of interest this proposal should be given sympathetic consideration. I hope some of the community groupings outlined in this debate will be accepted by the commission. In this way I feel improvements can be made in the good work which has already been done with a difficult and complicated assignment.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
I intend to speak in this debate only briefly in order to bring to the attention of the commission some of the problems arising from the changes suggested. The riding I have the honour to represent will be divided, and there will be two ridings in the area. This reflects the changes in population we have seen in southern Ontario, particularly in the Toronto and Hamilton areas, and is an indication of the industrial and residential growth of the region.
One of the main problems arising in connection with redistribution in Ontario is the confusion which arises between the provincial and the federal changes in the distribution of seats. As every member here is aware, this is inevitable unless the number of seats in the Ontario legislature and the number of seats in this place held by representatives from the
[Mrs. Wadds.l
province of Ontario become equal at some time.
The riding I represent has been divided in half. One of these halves was again divided into two parts, one of which will, virtually, become a riding in its own right; the other will become the riding of Wellington. I should like to refer in this connection to the township of Nassagaweya which did make representations to the electoral commission, though these representations were not reflected in the changes we now see before us. Like other members of this house I feel the commission appears not to have given consideration to the economic and geographical ties which exist in various areas. The town of Burlington which is to be in the new riding of Halton-Wentworth is closely linked with the township I have mentioned, Nassagaweya. The highways run north and south, and directly connect these two towns. The growth of the town of Burlington is toward Nassagaweya township. The people of Nassagaweya have shopped, farmed and grown up in this area and they wish to remain part of this area for all purposes.
As far as population figures are concerned, any change made to bring the township of Nassagaweya into the new riding would not be significant. The population of Burlington is approximately 50,000. Bringing in the township of Nassagaweya would perhaps add 2,500 people and 1,200 or 1,300 voters. I would therefore hope that the electoral boundaries commission would again consider, as it has promised to do in the past, bringing the township of Nassagaweya into this constituency in keeping with its growth, its history and its commercial habits, and keeping it tied closely with the town of Burlington.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
I am
sure it has been said before during this debate that no member has a vested interest in the part of Canada he represents in this house. While speaking tonight I shall try to express the feelings of the people of Simcoe county, as I have gathered them from many discussions since redistribution was first announced.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
We knew there had to be redistribution. We knew that changes would have to be made and that some ridings would have to be made larger. But we in Simcoe county did not think this would be done in the way in which it has been done in our part of Canada.
April 28, 1966

The objections which people in Simcoe county have are that the commission ignored population trends. They have made rural ridings so large that even now, before the ridings come into being, they are over what will be the population maximum in the redistribution which is only five years or perhaps less than five years away.
Most of all, in Simcoe county we feel that the redistribution commission has ignored completely community interest. They have splintered parts of Simcoe county into ridings in which the people have no community of interest whatsoever. In addition to that they have ignored geographical features. All of these are things which, as expressed in the act, should be taken into consideration. They have ignored the geographic section of Georgian bay and have joined together municipalities on the extreme west side of the bay with those on the east side of the bay; and yet they do not seem to have realized there is no connecting transportation link between them. They have ignored ethnic groupings. In the north part of our county we have an ethnic grouping of a township and a town. This is a very long standing grouping, and yet the commission has seen fit in its wisdom to divide these into two ridings.
To be specific, I should like to say something about the shape and size of Simcoe. It is a county bordering on Georgian bay. It is bounded by the waters of Georgian bay on the north and west and then by bodies of water like lake Simcoe and lake Couchiching on the east. Generally speaking the only land connection with the rest of Ontario is to the south. Simcoe county too has an interesting population. For electoral purposes in 1961 it had a population of about 143,000, almost an ideal figure for two rural ridings. As a matter of fact, in a brief presented by the county council of the county of Simcoe in respect of dividing the riding into a south and a north division, it was indicated that a good division could be made with 68,000 in the north riding and some 73,000 population in the south.
The county within these general geographical limits is divided into five community groups. Barrie is the largest community, a city of 24,000, right in the centre of the county. Orillia is another community group in the north, and in addition there are Midland, Penetang and Alliston. There always has been a great deal of county pride and county cohesion. Having regard to the good grouping, the many people in the county and the many 23033-284
Redistribution
officials, elected and otherwise, were astounded to find that instead of dividing Simcoe county into two good sized ridings, what happened was that in the northeast we have one very large riding which has a population of some 83,000 already, before it is formed into an area, and with the rate of growth it will be over the maximum before the change is made.
The remaining part of the riding was splintered into three other counties with which there is no close grouping at all. For example the municipality of Cresswell which borders on Barrie, which is the chief trading centre of the whole county, is now in a riding whose population centre is in the towns of Aurora and Newmarket. Camp Borden is a large military camp about ten miles out of Barrie. The people at Camp Borden divide their community contacts chiefly between Alliston and Barrie, although Barrie being the larger probably has the greatest contact. The personnel of Camp Borden very substantially look to the local members in that area as their members of parliament even though they do not always vote in the riding.
