Yet we have Camp Borden being put in a riding whose centre is Brampton. I do not know how many miles away it is, but I know that very few of the people who ever are stationed in Camp Borden have anything to do in or any contact with the town of Brampton. Yet Camp Borden and three municipalities now are in that riding. The same obtains in York North with Innisfil and its municipalities.
On the other side of the riding we have the municipalities of Flos, Christian Islands and Tiny which have no connection and not even a direct highway link with Owen Sound, and they now find themselves in the proposed riding of Grey-Simcoe. Perhaps the young men who drew these maps, and who I suspect drew them without looking at anything except the population, think that communication between Christian Islands and Owen Sound can be by war canoe, because it is about 130 miles by road.
These divisions are bad. They are bad not only from the point of view of community interest, but they are going to be bad for representation, because people are best represented in parliament who have a community of interest and who have some cohesion within the groups. We now find ourselves linked in splinters with the county of North York, the county of Peel and the county of Grey, whereas before we had just Dufferin

April 28. 1866
Redistribution
and Simcoe which were one cohesive political entity. It is true this is not a political division. No one speaks of this in terms of party politics, because in any of the areas concerned I do not think there is any very strong party trend one way or the other. However, in these days when we tend to have people who are disinterested in politics generally, sort of tearing them apart in a community sense I suggest is asking for more disinterest on the part of the people.
Perhaps it will be said, how are you going to do it; if you divide Simcoe county into the north and south what is going to happen to the spillover? I say the Electoral Boundaries Commission made a serious mistake, and that they should have given more consideration to the population trend. They should not have just looked at the 1951 and 1961 census and said, there is the trend. They should look at the trend today. In many instances suburban ridings should have been left toward the low end of the population level as required under the act, because the suburban ridings on the edges of cities are the rapidly growing ridings and are the places which will be affected most by the redistribution. There should have been room allowed for expansion in those ridings and room allowed to shift, because they will have to be changed anyway.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is quite proper for a riding in the centre of a city to have the maximum population allowed because it will not have to be changed during the next redistribution, but a riding such as North York and the new one named Peel South, which will incorporate a part of Simcoe North and Dufferin counties, should have been left at the lower end of the population scale, because by 1971 they will have grown to such an extent they will have to be divided into two ridings. Had they been left with the lowest possible population they could have been changed in 1961 without the massive dislocation that this redistribution is causing. I think this could and should have been done, and I think that the commission acted in a very arbitrary and shortsighted way in only looking at the population figures for 1951 and 1961, without giving consideration to geographic features, ethnic groupings and other matters of interest.
I do not think any great delay would be occasioned if the commission did give these matters serious reconsideration, and I am sure we would end up with many more Canadians vitally interested and concerned with politics at the riding level. I am sure we

would also have ridings designed in a better way.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is hard for me to approach this subject tonight in an unemotional and logical fashion when I realize that if redistribution is carried forward as presently planned the riding of Kent as such will disappear. I am certain that those many distinguished gentlemen who have had the honour of representing the county of Kent through the years, could they look over my shoulder tonight and see this new map as placed before us, would feel the same way I feel.
I should like to draw the attention of the commission to the fact that the county of Kent is one of the oldest and most historical in upper Canada. This county has a history which extends back to the year 1615 and we have a comprehensive recorded history of the workings of that county from the year 1626.
In order to be absolutely fair in my consideration of the action that is contemplated I did my best to tour completely through this district and ascertain the feelings of the people in this regard. They felt that if something had to be done it ought to be done. I assured them that I felt the same way, and that in order to have our democratic system progress, as we all wish it to do, following the policy of adequate representation, when-never there was an imbalance the necessary steps should be taken to correct it.
In touring this county I ascertained that the citizens are becoming somewhat impatient. Since the year 1867 the county of Kent has sent a representative to the House of Commons in Canada. When redistribution took place in 1903 the county of Kent was divided into East Kent and West Kent. When redistribution took place in 1914 East and Weat Kent were joined together as the county of Kent. From 1914 to 1965 the representative from that county has represented the entire county. Citizens of that area are now faced once again with a division of their favourite county.
Not only are the citizens faced once more with a division of the county, but they are faced with the disappearance of this designation of Kent as a riding in the province of Ontario. They are shocked and cannot understand why these two parts are to be renamed as Lambton-Kent and Essex, or why Kent is not used as the prefix of one or the other. Certainly if the renaming is justifiable, because of the size of the population, or for
April 28, 1966

alphabetical reasons, it is reasonable that the prefix "Kent" should be used in the designation of one of the new ridings. I support the citizens of the county of Kent in that view.
I wish personally to thank the commission for its early compliance with a representation which asked that the town of Tilbury be included as part of the riding which was formerly the county of Kent. The first map proposed placed the town of Tilbury in the Essex riding. Originally the town of Tilbury was located right on the border between the two counties. Representatives of that county have been of the opinion that since they have always been represented by the member for Kent they should continue to be so represented. I am very pleased, as are the citizens, that the new map has been drawn in such a way that Tilbury will once again fall within that part of the county of Kent.
I have always found the citizens of Kent to be reasonable, and accept with very little objection anything that they deem to be for the benefit of this country of ours, even though perhaps objectionable to themselves. However, at this time they fail to understand the necessity for dividing Kent. They feel that the city of Chatham, which lies almost in the centre of the county itself, and is in every respect the capital of that fair county, should have been considered as the focal point of any new riding created in that area. They feel that because of the development and growth of industry and population in that part of southwestern Ontario lying between lake St. Clair and lake Erie, the provisions set out in the present map will have to be changed when a new census is taken.
The people of that area feel very fortunate in that there is a close association between the cities in southern Ontario, including Sarnia, St. Thomas, Chatham and Windsor. In every case, except in respect of the division of the county of Kent, these cities were used as the focal points of the new ridings. The city of Chatham is located on the boundary line of the new riding of Kent-Essex. Just within the borders are located the towns of Tilbury and Kingsville. These are very fast growing towns. Leamington is also in this county, and it has almost reached the status of a city. It can be clearly seen that once a new census is taken consideration will have to be given as to whether or not these boundary lines will have to be changed again.
As I stated earlier my recommendations to the commission are made in as logical a manner as possible, and not on the basis of 23033-2841
Redistribution
my disappointment because of the disappearance of the riding. I have tried to point out what I feel are the justifiable changes in that area. It certainly was a shock to the citizens of the county of Kent when they found that the townships of Dover, Chatham, Orford, Howard and Harwich were added to the county of Lambton, with the city of Chatham being left in the riding of Kent-Essex. The townships of Raleigh, Tilbury East, Romney and Wheatley added the three townships in Essex county to form a new riding. Certainly they felt that the riding as it was before redistribution, with about 71,500 registered voters, was almost ideal and that the boundaries would be left as they were.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I think this in itself was the most striking feature in the news of the new map, so far as the citizens of the area were concerned. They felt that since they did comply in nearly every respect with what might be considered the optimum riding, with the boundaries following very closely county lines, lying between two lakes, Lake St. Clair in the northwest and Lake Erie in the south, and having the city of Chatham at its centre, which is the natural focal point for all business and social life in that particular area, and with the ideal number of 71,500 registered voters, redistribution would not touch them in any respect.
However, Mr. Speaker, they are facing this very philosophically. They feel that if it must come, and if it is for the benefit of the country, they will accept it. But they do request that the commission look once again at this very important matter to see whether the ridings could be drawn in such a way in this part of Ontario so as to mean that Chatham could once again be the central point, which logically one would expect it to be, for the riding. The people of the area also ask that the name Kent county be retained. Failing to do this, may I respectfully request that the commission-and I know their task
has been an unpopular and difficult one____give
every consideration to the representation made on behalf of the citizens of Kent county that the name Kent, which is so dear to the people in the area, and which has served Canada so well in its history in every respect be retained at least as the prefix of one of the new ridings.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter this debate, but do so for three reasons. The first

April 28. 1866
Redistribution
reason is that the chairman of the commission said, as reported in the Toronto Star of January 20, 1965, that many of the ridings will have to be redrawn in 1972 when the next federal election is scheduled, and the people who do the job in 1972 will have a difficult time of it again. In view of the electoral boundaries of Halton-Wentworth I believe I may be able to offer an alternative solution which will mean that in 1972 these people will not have such a difficult time.
The second reason is that the electoral boundaries fixed for the provincial riding have already been changed after representation in the provincial house, and I believe that if there were factors influencing the change at that time, they should again be emphasized so that a change may be made in the proposed federal riding of Halton-Wentworth.
Third, the people of Ancaster have shown such concern that I should also like to speak on their behalf for just a minute. I might at this point add that the chairman mentioned that about 200 briefs were placed before the commission last June and about 70 of them were purely formal. The municipality of Ancaster admitted that the brief they placed before the commission at that time was of a purely formal nature. At no time did they have any idea that they would not be included in the Hamilton metro area, so on a false assumption they presented a rather formal brief, which they now realize may have been a mistake.
The terms of reference laid down for the Electoral Boundaries Commission were, of course, to limit the population to 70,000, with a 25 per cent tolerance figure, or a total of 87,000 in any one riding. Further, the commission were to take into consideration existing sociological and geographical connections within the various ridings. It is with regard to the sociological relationship that Ancaster has with the rest of the Hamilton metro area that I should like to speak.
Ancaster is an integral part of the county of Wentworth. They share administered services such as health and welfare, the administration of justice, the Hamilton-Wentworth S burban Roads Commission, the Hamilton-Wentworth Planning Area Board, the Mutual Aid Fire Services Association, the joint county library system and the county assessment system commencing January, 1967, to name only a few.
Those who reside in Ancaster township spend much of their daily life within the
[Mr. Morison.l
confines of Hamilton. Most of these people work in Hamilton, do their shopping in Hamilton, read the Hamilton daily papers, listen to the Hamilton radio stations, watch Hamilton television and go to Hamilton for their entertainment. The tradesmen who call on them come from Hamilton. Those who deliver oil, coal, milk and bread are Hamilton tradesmen. I believe that in future the Ancaster area will be included in the Hamilton area as annexation takes place.
Much as they would like to be kept in the Hamilton area as an integral or single unit, these people understand that because of the population figures in the area this is impossible. At the present time the Brantford riding has approximately 77,500 people; Hamilton-Mountain, 79,200; Halton-Wentworth, 73,100; Hamilton West, 79,700; Hamilton-Wentworth, 71,500; and Wellington, 68,600. The population of Ancaster township is approximately 16,500.
If we accept that it cannot as a township be included in any of the ridings I have mentioned, then let us look for an alternate solution that might carry on into the 1972 realignment of electoral boundaries. The alternate, which as I say is a second choice which might be considered, is as follows: First, by drawing a line from the township's northern boundary, southerly along Binkley's road, then along the line between lots 37 and 38 to the Jerseyville road, continuing southerly along Shaver's side road across highways No. 2 and 53 to Butter's road, and continuing southerly along Penny's road and Moffat road to the southwestern boundary of the township.
You will note that this forms an almost perfectly straight line across the township as a continuation of the dividing line between the federal ridings of Wellington and Halton-Wentworth to the north, and almost connecting to the dividing line between the federal ridings of Brantford and Hamilton-Wentworth to the south.
The population in this western portion of the township so created is estimated at approximately 3,400, and this part would remain in the federal riding of Brantford. The population of the Brantford riding would thereby be reduced to approximately 64,500, leaving them room to negotiate for the inclusion of their western area for which they originally asked. The residents of this part of the township do have at least some affinity with the Brantford area. Some of them work near Brantford, shop in Brantford, read the Brantford newspapers and are on Brantford
April 28, 1966

telephone exchanges, and there is no real
dissatisfaction with the fact that they have been included in the Brantford riding.
[DOT] (9:30 D.m.)
Second, you take a line drawn from Shaver's sideroad along the new highway 403 right-of-way to the eastern boundary of the township of Ancaster at the Hamilton city limits, and you would further divide the township of federal electoral purposes. The population of the southeastern portion so created is estimated at approximately 3,000. This could be added to the federal riding of Hamilton Mountain. The population of Hamilton Mountain would thus be increased to approximately 82,000, which is still well within the 87,000 maximum permitted.
Highway 403, as proposed, makes a natural and logical boundary line. The township does not anticipate much development south of this highway because of the problems involved in providing municipal services once the highway construction is completed. I understand that there have been negotiations or it is expected this will be the first area of Ancaster township expropriated by Hamilton.
The population of the remaining northeastern portion of the township is estimated at approximately 10,000 people. This could be added to the federal riding of Halton-Wentworth. The population of Halton-Wentworth would thus be increased to approximately 83,000, which is also within the
87,000	maximum permitted.
This part of the township includes all of the primary development area, and the problems and the way of life here are very similar to the problems and way of life of the people of Dundas and Burlington, who are already included in the Hamilton-Wentworth riding. Our sociological and geographical ties with those areas, as well as with the city of Hamilton, would be maintained and protected.
The people of Ancaster are now part of a federal riding which is made up of these and other suburban areas. There is no objection or discontent. They will not lose their affinity with the city of Hamilton. They will remain represented by a member of parliament from the Hamilton area which, of course, they feel is of paramount importance.
I believe that the changes proposed by myself, and certainly the changes that have been requested by the residents of the area can be made very easily without affecting any other riding. The only change involved
Redistribution
would be a change in the riding boundaries within the township of Ancaster, and this should not cause the commission any undue amount of difficulty. I ask, then, that the commission review the decision to add Ancaster township to Brant county, and that they look with some understanding on the recommendations that I have made, knowing that this work can be done without disturbing the electoral boundaries as laid down for the federal ridings, and also with the idea that if they look at the projected growth in the areas, they will find that in 1972 they have simplified the job for any future commission that may have to undertake this work.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSION REPORTS
speechtext:
In
rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I do so with a very sad heart. I can certainly say that since the report and the new maps were published by the commission, my heart has been saddened. The commission has seen fit to eliminate and chop up the historic riding of Hastings-Frontenac. I want to remind the house that it was to this great riding our first settlers came to Canada, acquired land and helped to develop this great country. When I first presented the report and map published by the commission, someone said that had a father given his children a map of Canada and a pair of scissors and asked them to cut out a jig-saw puzzle that would be difficult to put together, they could not have done a better job than the commission did.
At the outset, I want to say that I agree with some of the members of the other place who have stated redistribution should have been handled by the senators. This could have been done at very little expense to our taxpayers, and I feel these men were much more competent to handle this duty than were the commissioners.
In so far as redistribution is concerned, Mr. Speaker, it occurs in Canada every ten years following the decennial census. Numerical equality is the basis upon which redistribution is planned. In order to ensure the continuity of political structures, however, the boundaries of electoral districts should be varied as little as is absolutely necessary. Redistribution, as it has been proposed by this commission, should it occur every ten years would mean the end of political organizations in this country. It is submitted that there has never been such a complete redistribution in this country as that which is now

April 28, 1986
Redistribution
proposed, not even in the days of the infamous gerrymandering.
It is not suggested that this redistribution is not necessary, but it is submitted that redistribution of this magnitude occurring every ten years would be a serious detriment to political organizations. It is therefore in the interests of preventing a recurring redistribution of this proportion that the commission should establish electoral boundaries which would enable the newly created electoral districts to accommodate expanding population with a minimum of operation of those boundaries. This commission cannot be expected to foresee the extent of the population increase that will occur in all areas of Ontario within the next quarter of a century. However, the drafting of electoral districts, taking into consideration the trend of the population expansion that has been experienced during the past quarter century, could do a great deal in helping to alleviate the need for substantial redistributions during the next quarter century.
Experience has shown also that population expansion in eastern Ontario, with the exception of certain areas, has been greatest along the north shore of lake Ontario. It is submitted therefore that the electoral districts fronting on lake Ontario should be organized to allow for expected continuing expansion. It is noted also that in the proposed redistribution, the electoral district with the greatest population will be York-Sear borough with a population of some 80,000. The electoral district with the least population will be Thunder Bay with a population of some 53,000. Along the lake front east of metropolitan Toronto the constituencies and their populations are as follows: Ontario riding, 63,432; Oshawa, 79,240; Northumberland-Durham, 62,912; Prince Edward-Hastings, 69,692; Kingston and The Islands, 79,838; Leeds, 62,656.
[DOT] (9:40 D.m.)
To the north of these constituencies lie the ridings which reach into the hinterland of Ontario which, with their populations, are: Victoria-Haliburton, 55,055; Hastings, 60,454; Frontenac-Addington, 55,638; Renfrew-Lan-ark, 55,418. Omitted from this list is Peterborough with a population of 70,422. These ridings along the lakefront should be distributed so that the proposed population will be reduced to nearer the minimum, and the population directed into the ridings to the north. This will enable the expected expansion of population to bring the lakefront

electoral districts into numerical equality of representation without the need for boundary alteration.
Under the now proposed redistribution the townships of Belmont and Methuen and the village of Havelock will be included in the constituency of Victoria-Haliburton. Havelock is situated on provincial highway No. 7 east of the city of Peterborough and 52 miles from the town of Lindsay, which is the major population centre for the riding of Victoria-Haliburton.
There is no road connecting Havelock with the rest of the riding other than one to the north, and this road is really not a very good road. To reach Lindsay, the residents of Havelock and the township must travel through the proposed riding of Peterborough. Likewise, the sitting member for Victoria-Haliburton, to reach his constituents in Belmont and Methuen and Havelock, would have to drive right through the riding of Peterborough. Also, the residents of Havelock have no community of interest with Lindsay. They are attracted to Peterborough for economic, social and cultural purposes. It is submitted that the townships of Belmont and Methuen and the village of Havelock should form a part of the proposed riding of Peterborough.
For years now these two townships and the village of Havelock have formed part of Peterborough county. Under the new set-up for the Ontario provincial ridings they will remain part of Peterborough riding. The towns are six miles apart and their churches are served by the same priests or ministers. They have the same schoolboards, the same health units, the same county councils, which I think is very important to consider, Mr. Speaker.
We who made representations in Toronto to the commission and pointed out the necessity for having these two townships of Belmont and Methuen, and Havelock, put into the riding of Peterborough, left the meeting very satisfied that the judge and the commission had concurred in our proposition. We were really astounded when we found out that this was not true.
I should mention here that I hope the commission will really show some interest in these representations. Anybody looking at a map of the area would realize that this is the proper thing to do. What bothers me most is that I learned that the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was cut up, but when
April 28, 1365

the top brass or those in authority made representations it was changed back again. I think that some of the other ridings should also be changed back.
In summarizing, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to make a few points. Democratic government is dependant upon effective political parties. To be effective, political parties require organization. Political organization requires consistent geographical units based on community of interest and population centres. In establishing the electoral district boundaries, not only should numerical factors be taken into consideration; geographical factors must be considered to enable the elected representative effectively to represent his constituency and to encourage the citizens to become involved in political activity in their areas. Reducing the population in those areas in which expansion is expected to be greatest will allow expansion without the need of alteration of electoral boundaries, thereby preventing a disruption of political organization.

I consider it a great honour and privilege to be asked to make these few remarks, and I can assure you that this is the last time that I or anyone else will have to pinch hit for this great area, in connection with this particular problem of redistribution.
Before I proceed to speak about the metropolitan area of Toronto I should like to make one or two brief remarks about the .-hanges which have occurred in my own (Mr. Aiken.]
riding of Wellington South. First of all, we are happy that the name of Wellington has been retained. We have dropped the word "south" and we are sorry to lose the townships of Erin and Pilkington, as well as Erin village and Elora village. We are also happy that the commission paid attention to the recommendation we made to it, in that we felt that the township of Dumfries would be much better in the riding of Brantford, and this is where it is remaining. I am sure that the people in both ridings will be very satisfied.
The hon. member for Halton mentioned that Nassagaweya township should remain there, and I am sure that the inhabitants would be slightly more at home in the Halton riding because of the Burlington area being their shopping centre. For this reason and others we have no objections to them staying in Halton. I think that we could exchange the people at the north end of Halton, Erin township, because I think they would be happier to stay in Wellington. As the hon. member representing the riding I say that I am sorry to lose the ones we are losing and happy to receive those who are coming into the riding.
My remarks about Toronto, of course, Mr. Speaker, will be brief as I am sure the hon. members of this house would not expect me to be as familiar with the electoral district of metropolitan Toronto as someone who lived in that area. My observations are based on the findings and recommendations from meetings that have been held there by Conservative candidates and Conservative associations in the ridings. There are 22 ridings in this great area of almost 2 million people. I think that the commission has done a reasonably good job in dividing it up into ridings.
With respect to the riding of Scarborough East, the objection is with respect to the westerly boundary of the proposed riding. The area bounded by Ellesmere road, Markham, Lawrence avenue east and McCowans Road should be put into Scarborough East, and an area comparable in size should be put into Scarborough West.
With respect to the Scarborough West riding, the objection is to the easterly and northerly boundaries. In connection with York-Scarborough, the objection of the committee in this area is to the easterly and northerly boundaries of the proposed riding. In York East the objection is to the northerly and westerly boundaries of the proposed riding. The western boundary should follow the
April 28, 1966

Don river boundary as much as possible. In the Greenwood and Broadview ridings the objections are chiefly about the boundary lines.
In Rosedale the objection would seem to be twofold. The first objection is to the southerly boundary of the riding, and specifically to the important waterfront area which, in the committee's view, should be kept in one unit. Second, objection is taken to the name, as they feel Rosedale is only one small residential area in what is otherwise a large riding. They feel that this name should be changed to St. Paul's riding, as there is a considerable historical association with that name in this general area.
Similarly, in Trinity and Davenport the objections are chiefly directed to the boundaries. The same objections apply to Park-dale. The hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) apparently objects to the name. The objection with respect to the Humber-Valley riding is to the northern and western boundaries, for geographic reasons.
I wish I had time to enlarge upon some of these, but time is running out, and I can just mention some of the objections in relation to the various boundaries. In the Etobicoke area the objection is a little more pronounced. Here the committee feels that that portion of the proposed electoral district of Etobicoke which lies east of the Humber river should not be included in Etobicoke, for the following reasons. The first is that the Humber river is a natural boundary which for many years has served as the dividing line between the ridings of York West and York Centre.

of the geographical or provincial constituencies, avoiding confusion in the minds of voters when federal or provincial elections are held.
In York South, no great objection arises. In Eglinton the objection is to the westerly and northerly boundaries of the proposed riding. The dividing of such a long established community as Eglinton, which has maintained its identity both as ward 9 in the city of Toronto and as a provincial and federal riding for many years, is regretted, and we ask for the reconsideration of this division if possible.
In the case of the other ridings, the objections are chiefly to the boundaries which have been proposed. Generally speaking, I would say the commission has done a reasonably good job. Its task was not easy. Constituencies would have been happier had the commission not disregarded historical factors and municipal divisions. Wherever possible the commission should take a second look so that municipal, provincial and federal representatives serve the same area. Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to support my colleague the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) and to present as briefly as I can the objections raised by some considerable number of my constituents with regard to certain proposed changes in the electoral district of Algoma West which it has been my privilege to represent in this house for the past 26 years.
The objection, in brief, is to the cutting off of the township of Michipicoten from Algoma West and annexing it to Cochrane riding. This is most impractical because of the almost insurmountable difficulties in travel and communication between the Michipicoten area and the Cochrane riding.
I think this is plainly shown when we realize that to drive by car from Kapuskas-ing, the seat of the member in Cochrane riding, to Wawa, whether it be via North Bay to the east or by Nipigon to the west, the distance would be approximately 700 miles either way. To travel by rail, even without considering the inconvenience of delays due to train connections, the distance would be about 300 miles. Compared with the foregoing, between Wawa and Sault Ste. Marie, a distance of approximately 140 miles, there is a daily bus service over the Trans-Canada highway.
The population of Michipicoten township, according to the 1961 census is 4,439. In Wawa, the largest community centre in Michipicoten township, the main source of employment is iron ore mining. It is the site of the Algoma Ore Properties, a subsidiary of the Algoma Steel Company of Sault Ste. Marie. The interests of these people are tied completely with Sault Ste. Marie, and to support this I would like to quote from a representation make by the reeve of Michipicoten township:
Until highway No. 17 was opened to the north of Lake Superior, we, in this mining area, lived in isolation. Then, as now, our ties were with Sault Ste. Marie. Economically, socially and politically, we are tied with Sault Ste. Marie. We wish to

register our objections, in the strongest terms to block this move to return us to isolation-political isolation.
We speak for nearly 5,000 who inhabit this progressive mining community and tourist area. We have no desire to become the backwoods fringe of any constituency.

Reeve, Municipality of Michipicoten.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in northern Ontario we have been concerned with the major fact that many of the outlying areas are finding themselves

attached to a riding to which they have no connection. I am well aware that the job which faced the Electoral Boundaries Commission was difficult, and I think in the main that it has done a very good job. I think it is also true that in northern Ontario the commission may have failed to take into consideration the lines of communication which have been established. I particularly agree with the suggestions which have been made by the hon. member for Cochrane, who has s riding now stretching not only from James bay but from Hudson bay to lake Superior. 1 think everyone will realize that there are sections in this riding which have a much closer affinity with other areas than with the central area of the Cochrane riding.
It is a fact that we have established tolerances. It is a good thing, probably, that at the same time in northern Ontario the ridings have been balanced to within several thousand persons in each of them. I think none of us in northern Ontario will object if the problems which have been raised by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) and the hon. member for Algoma West (Mr. Nixon) are taken into consideration.
I think it is unreasonable that the areas lying on the outskirts of Sault Ste. Marie, and certainly either through radio participation or transportation systems, within the ambit of that centre, which unites them with Sault Ste. Marie, should belong to the far north and be attached to the ridings there.
Our interest in this matter is not a close one. I have had little connection with the people of most of that area, but I am aware of the fact that we have an obligation in northern Ontario to take into consideration the large distances involved in order to provide as good representation as is possible for all the constituents we may have.
I think an exception could be made in northern Ontario, without coming near the limits which have been laid down in the redistribution act, so as to take into consideration matters of transportation. I should like to draw attention to several areas. I would refer to the two towns of Bowden and Nor-dica west of Cochrane which come into the Timmins area. These are very small communities, which have been within the ambit of the Cochrane riding for a number of years, and which, because of transportation lines, would be connected with the Cochrane riding. Only a few miles to the other side of the riding would be needed to take in these towns.
April 28. 1966

There are no other towns in that area and there are not likely to be. I therefore suggest the boundary should be shifted to the east to take these towns into the Cochrane riding. I further suggest that at least the town of Foleyet and the other small communities on the Foleyet-Chapleau highway, to reach which the member representing Cochrane would have to leave the northern section of his riding, come through Timmins riding and pass through that riding, should remain in Timmins. Their total population is not more than a few thousand people.
We have an advantage in this area because we all use the same television station in Timmins. It already has five satellites. If this is used as one of the criteria, a great deal of northern Quebec would be included because several of these satellites are situated there. In view of these communications and transportation facilities I suggest a trade should be made of these two communities east of Cochrane in exchange for the Foleyet area, which must obviously be served by Timmins. Because there is a connecting road to Chapleau, I suggest this town, too, should be included in the Timmins riding.
I am sympathetic to the people in Jamestown and I hope an arrangement can be made whereby they can be included in the Algoma riding. If this cannot be done, there might be a readjustment of the northern boundaries of Sault Ste. Marie so as to include all those people who are normally connected with that community. If no other action can be taken, then I would ask that the boundaries of my riding be extended both in the north and in the south to Lake Superior. This would mean that the areas in close proximity to Sault Ste. Marie would be cut off from the Cochrane riding by my riding and would obviously have to be placed in another area. I am not offering very much by suggesting this. It is true I am adding some territory to my riding but as far as I know there are no people living in this region.
The suggestions made with regard to northern Ontario are truly non-partisan. All of us who represent ridings in northern Ontario are concerned about the new areas we are getting, not because we do not want them but because there will be a realignment of the communities in the new areas. This is inevitable. We should have liked things to remain as they were, because over the years people have developed attachments to their ridings. But that is not possible. I welcome the many
Redistribution
communities which have been added to Ti-miskaming and I believe the changes I have recommended, and the changes recommended by the other members from Ontario which I have endorsed, will be in the interest of all. It is my hope they will bring the best representation possible to all who live in the constituencies concerned. As to Cochrane, any concession in northern Ontario will have to be made there, as well as, to some extent, in the Port Arthur area because the area is so vast that service is a difficult proposition at the present time.
[DOT] (10:40 D.m.)
In my opinion these suggestions will make some adjustment in the geographical sense rather than really change the population figures, with which I think most members are quite pleased and agree will bring a great deal more stability to the representation which can be provided. As the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) mentioned, I know that the people who have sat on the commission in Ontario have been familiar with the problem as it has developed provincially and will be aware of the areas of which we speak. They may feel, because of this discussion, that some support should be given to the idea of the geographical changes, if only to reestablish the lines of communication which are normal, and in most cases possible only if certain small changes take place.
I certainly recommend these changes to the commission and hope they will give some consideration to them. I hope they also will know, when I make the suggestions in respect of the Timmins riding, that the people there are aware of the fact that in adding on these areas the responsibility is increasing and they are willing to shoulder that responsibility for the purpose of providing better representation for the individuals who are being dislocated in this redistribution.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-CONSTRUCTION OF REPLICA OF "GRANDE HERMINE" FOR EXPO '67.
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-CONSTRUCTION OF REPLICA OF "GRANDE HERMINE" FOR EXPO '67.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is essential that in order to debate the question of the "Grande Hermine" I must first of all establish the fact that Gaspe is the birthplace of Canada.
It is unfortunate that there is such a diversity of opinion amongst our historians as to who discovered Canada. This is possibly due to the evident distortions of history that appear when we read the English and French versions of our Canadian history. How can anyone claim that Cabot, the Venetian navigator, claimed the land for Henry VII of England?
Jacques Cartier, after reaching this side of the Atlantic, stopped in Newfoundland, in Labrador, on the shores of northern Quebec, and then came through the Magdalen Islands up to the Baie de Chaleur finally arriving in the bay of Gaspe on July 24, 1534. He raised a cross 30 feet in height, placed thereon a shield embossed with three fleurs-de-lis and took possession of the land in the name of the King of France. There was no war at that time. I am sure that if the land had been taken in the name of the King of England there would have been a war in 1534, but there is no history of any such war having taken place.
I will not dwell long on this fact. Suffice it to say that historians agree that any crosses which he may have placed elsewhere on this soil were only landmarks and not similar to the one at Gaspe upon which he placed a
April 28, 1966	COMMONS
shield with the fleur-de-lis. Nowhere in history is it related that he took possession at another landing.
Four hundred years later in 1934 the governments of France, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada commemorated this event by the erection of a 110-ton cross carved out of granite, and by other ceremonies, at Gaspe. Present at that time were the Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Cardinal Villeneuve of Quebec, Sir Roger Keyes, representing England, Mr. Flandin, the minister of public works, representing France, Hon. W. D. Robbins, ambassador from United States in Canada, and Hon. L. A. Taschereau, premier of Quebec.
Mr. Flandin has stated that Cartier took possession of Canada at Gaspe. Mr. Trudel, one of our better known contemporary historians puts forth the argument in the following words:
It is clear from the importance of the ceremony that the cross (at Gaspe) was intended to indicate that a territory was being taken possession of in the name of Francois ler.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
The greatest proof for acceptance of this historical fact is the precedent of 1934 and it should be accepted as such. Marc Laterreur is also of the same opinion.
Since 1957, and I am sure the files of the Department of Northern Affairs will prove my statement, our Gaspe Historical Society under the chairmanship of L'Abbe Michel Le Moignan and the Historical Sites Commission under the presidency of Wilf M. Carter have endeavoured to obtain recognition of this fact and make of Gaspe an historic site.
A few years later, in 1961 to be exact, the Jubilee branch of the Canadian Legion at Gaspe, under Mr. Albert Cassidy and district chairman G. Lacouver, believed that if Gaspe were declared an historic site the construction of a replica of the Grande Hermine would be symbolic gesture aiding the development of the site and contributing to the economic advantages so desired for that region of our country.
Petitions were signed to this effect, there was correspondence with Richard Holden of McKay and Holden, who had incorporated a private company under the name La Societe de Navigation La Grande Hermine Limitee, Mr. Kniewasser of Expo '67, the present builders of the ship, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Commerce, the Centennial Commission, the Provincial
DEBATES	4491
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Secretary of Quebec-in fact, with all those who would be interested in contributing to the construction of the replica of the Grande Hermine so that it would be first of all a source of attraction at Expo '67 and eventually find a permanent berth at Gaspe, the birth place of Canada.
To our disappointment we find a press release of March 18 from the minister's office advising us of his decision to have the ship built elsewhere and given a final resting place at Quebec city. After four years we find that the whole plan, which originated in Gaspe, was scuttled and a declaration to the effect that the ship would find a permanent berth at the Cartier-Brebeuf Park, in Quebec, which after all can only commemorate the second voyage of Cartier to the Canadian shores.
The price announced by the minister is not in keeping with correspondence which we now have and which we will speak of on another occasion. It is now found that the ship will have to be dismantled in order to find its berthing place at Quebec and engineers are going to be hired to study the feasibility of dismantling it.
What problems we encounter when we are creating a complete distortion of our Canadian history to give to Quebec city another historical monument. All municipal councils, public bodies, economic councils, Canadian Legion branches and other societies condemn this decision.
An article originating in Quebec city in Le Soleil and written by Odilon Arteau condemns this decision and states categorically that the Grande Hermine should find a haven at Gaspe. If the city of Quebec believes that the haven and final resting place of this ship should be Gaspe, we cannot understand why the department has announced that it will be Quebec city.
I trust that the minister will not be associated with this decision, that it will be rescinded, and above all and most important, that he will recommend that the question of the birthpla e of Canada come before the standing committee of the house which deals with matters relating to his department.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I refer the minister to a booklet prepared by the Natural Resources Intelligence Service, Department o) the Interior, in 1926. This booklet, produced by a department of government, states, when speaking of the Gaspe peninsula:
The peninsula may be said to be, historically, the oldest part of Canada, for it was on its shores
4492	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion near the town of Gaspe that Jacques Cartier, in the year 1534, landed and claimed the country for his sovereign, the King of France.
I have here letters dated 1961 and addressed to the museum of Saint-Malo, France, to architects in France and to Mr. Kniewasser of Expo '67. All these letters claim that the Grande Hermine should be built and berthed at Gaspe. Who has stolen our idea? This is what we would be very interested to know.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-CONSTRUCTION OF REPLICA OF "GRANDE HERMINE" FOR EXPO '67.
speechtext:
As was announced in a press release from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources on March 18, 1966, the federal government intends to construct a detailed full scale replica of Jacques Cartier's ship, the Grande Hermine. The ship will be on display at Expo '67, where it will be a prominent feature of the development called La Ronde. There is no doubt, as the minister has been quoted as saying, the Grande Hermine will be a major historical contribution to Expo '67.
After Expo '67, the intention is to move the vessel to Quebec city where it will be established as the focal feature of Cartier-Brebeuf National Historic Park. In planning the interpretation of national historic sites, it is imperative to keep in mind the precise nature of the event to be commemorated. There is no doubt that during the wintering episode in Cartier's second voyage, the outstanding event is the fact that his vessel laid at anchor for an entire season at the confluence of the Lairet and St. Charles rivers. This is the site of Cartier-Brebeuf park.
Cartier-Brebeuf, Mr. Speaker, has a specific connection with Jacques Cartier of greater duration than Gaspe has. He wintered at the site of Cartier-Brebeuf park, and this wintering is the first documented one for any large body of Europeans in mainland Canada.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-PICTOU LANDING, N.S.- REPORTED UNSAFE CONDITION OF WHARF
TRANSPORT-PICTOU LANDING, N.S.- REPORTED UNSAFE CONDITION OF WHARF
speechtext:
I rise at this time with regard to a question which I put to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) a few days ago concerning a very mundane but important matter in my own constituency, namely the repairs to the wharf at Pictou landing. The condition has worsened since I asked the minister the question,

DEBATES	April 28, 1966
which was ruled out at that time by Mr. Speaker. It was for this reason I raised the matter during this debate.
The company which was exporting pulp from the area, the Henderson Lumber Company, sent a telegram to the minister and various representations have been made by me as member for the area. The reasons I am putting forward for the reconstruction of this wharf are twofold: First, in so far as this economy is concerned, the area is a designated one and the export of pulp from this area is providing work for truckers, stevedores and so on, numbering approximately 100 men. In addition, the Henderson Lumber Company has given out information they have looked at this area as the possible site of a sawmill which would provide further work and further export of lumber.
This wharf is important, too, in that a number of fishermen use it for lobster and other types of fishing. During the last short period of time when the wharf was under temporary and minor repairs commencing last fall, the contract was about half completed when a crane went through the end of the wharf. I think perhaps the old Latin phrase, res ipsa loquitur, the thing speaks for itself, is applicable to this situation. We were shown that these repairs were necessary. I must say that the Minister of Public Works has always been very good and advised me whenever I have made inquiries about work that was to be done.
If I might make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works, it would be this: The suggestion arises out of something brought forward by his predecessor, a gentleman now in the other place, Senator J. P. Deschatelets, in correspondence with me in the year 1964. At that time consideration was being given to carrying out wharf reconstruction in the Pictou landing area. The minister of that day pointed out to me that this would be considered in the estimates for the operating year, and it would involve shortening the existing structure by some 100 feet.
[DOT] (11:00 p.m.)
That is the suggestion I put forward to the minister tonight, that he ask his officials to look into this question and to carry out this reconstruction and, if necessary, to cut off a bit of the wharf-100 feet or whatever is necessary-which was the suggestion of the former minister. I have looked at the wharf and have been making submissions about it for many years, because frankly I do not
April 28. 1966	COMMONS
believe that as the wharf now stands it is necessary. It is a long structure, and for the good of the shipping of pulp, possible lumber shipments and also for the good of the fishermen who use it I hope that the minister will immediately have his officials go to the area and look into the question of its complete reconstruction.
I realize the main estimates for this year have been tabled but I hope that consideration will be given by way of supplementary estimates to carrying out the necessary reconstruction. I suggest it is no longer just a matter of minor repairs but of extensive repairs. As I have pointed out, perhaps this could be done by way of cutting off part of the wharf and working on the balance of it. I was in the area during the Easter recess and minor repairs and dredging were being carried out so that fishermen would have a place to fish from during the lobster season. This was being done all inside the wharf. From the outer or north end it has been getting worse from time to time; the piles are rotten.
I submit to the minister, who I know will take it into consideration, that reconstruction of this wharf, a very important link in the east Pictou area, should be proceeded with as quickly as possible.
Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for drawing this matter to my attention. There is a good deal of uncertainty about the suitability of this large wharf for local requirements. It has been used mainly by a group of inshore fishermen and to a limited extent by exporters of softwood pulpwood.
Over the years the structure has deteriorated to the point that in May, 1965 it was necessary to reduce the load limit by 50 per cent. Early last winter an effort was made to have minor repairs made, mainly to accommodate the fishermen and also the ferry service; but at that time it was found that the wharf was in such a bad state of repair that it had to be closed to vehicular traffic on February 10, 1966. The cost of putting this wharf in good condition is estimated at $200,000.
I assume that the structure was allowed to deteriorate over the years because of the uncertainty about how well it would suit future needs. The requirement of the local fishery could be met better at a considerably lower cost, and this possibility is being explored. However, the kind of structure that would suit the fishermen probably would not be useful for the export of pulpwood. About
DEBATES	4493
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
7,000	cords of wood have been loaded there annually in recent years. Moreover, so far we have been unable to get any information that promises an increase in the export of this commodity at this location. It would not be reasonable to make a major expenditure to facilitate this export without some assurance that the economic justification of that expenditure would not vanish within a few years.
The Henderson Lumber Company has known about the deterioration of the wharf over the years. It is most regrettable that the company has bought a quantity of wood for shipment during 1966 from this site; however, even if we felt that we could justify the major expenditure to which I have referred, the wharf could not be reconstructed in time for this year's shipment. The structure is being examined to see what can be done to make it suitable for use by the fishermen during this season. The larger question indicated by the hon. member is one that I shall pursue thoroughly.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCONTINUANCE OF STEAMSHIP "CANORA" ON WEST COAST
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCONTINUANCE OF STEAMSHIP "CANORA" ON WEST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first of all state correctly the question I asked the Minister of Transport three days ago because there was an error in it at that time. I sent the minister a corrected version yesterday which is as follows:
In view of the fact that the Canadian National Railways has decided to discontinue operation of the S.S. Canora on the west coast, causing unemployment for approximately 50 men;
And in view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway has now decided to operate their own vessel in this service;
Will the Minister of Transport intercede with the Canadian National Railways to replace the Canora with another vessel, owned by the Company and operated by their present long-term employees?
I should like to indicate that this is a grave situation affecting approximately 50 men and their families.
On April 5 the Canadian Merchant Service Guild, an organization of marine officers, was informed that the Canadian National was going to discontinue the operation of the S.S. Canora, a vessel which has operated from the B.C. mainland to Vancouver Island since 1918. That is 48 years of service. The ship employs approximately 50 men, including 12 officers, many of them with very long continuous service. In fact, the service of the officers averages out to 20.7 years per man.
April 28. 1966
4494	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The guild was invited by the management to attend meetings to discuss the future of employees. They met with courtesy, and spoke of the courteous reception given to them. Members of management made suggestions which included such things as job transfers to other areas, retraining, early and deferred retirements, but made clear that it could give no guarantee to any employee about a position in the service.
The men feel that because of seniority groupings now in effect in the railway system, possible replacement within that system is therefore improbable. They feel that to be forced to retire early, especially in the case of officers, would cost them hundreds of dollars because early retirement would force them to take a lower pension with which they would have to be satisfied for the rest of their lives.
It is not as though there was a reason to discontinue the service. It is not redundant, it is necessary. The Canadian National plans that it will be continued by a commercial carrier. Tenders for the service have now been invited. Second, another company will operate the service and will still make a fair profit. Third, the Canadian Pacific has a very similar operation which has been handled for them by F. M. Yorke & Son Limited, a Vancouver based firm.
Recently the Canadian Pacific has decided to operate this service with its own vessel, which is expected to be ready for operation by approximately May 15, 1966. This is the vessel for which tenders have been called.
It appears that the Canadian National is now going to make the mistake originally made by the Canadian Pacific in the use of a commercial carrier. In this situation I feel that the minister should intercede with the

Canadian National and urge upon that body the need to replace the Canora with another vessel owned by the Canadian National and operated by its present long-term employees.
This is a very serious problem and the men are most anxious that the government take action before they are thrown out, and before it is too late to embody their services again within the system.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister without Portfolio):
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCONTINUANCE OF STEAMSHIP "CANORA" ON WEST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of
Transport made inquiries of the Canadian National Railways. I can sympathize with the position outlined by the hon. member who has just spoken.
The information given to the minister was that the S.S. Canora has been in the island service on the west coast, and that the vessel indeed is 48 years old, as mentioned by the hon. member. However, it cannot be operated in the present service beyond May or June of this year. Therefore in order to continue to provide a service, the company is seeking alternative means of carrying out its obligations. This involves the retirement of the Canora from service.
The minister was also advised by the railway that the railway company considers it uneconomic to make the capital expenditure necessary to buy a new vessel and that in any case it would be impossible to secure one without considerable delay. The employees involved, and who may be displaced, have been notified. Discussions have been held with the general chairman of the union, and everything possible is being done to reassign the personnel displaced to other jobs.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.13 p.m.

Friday, April 29, 1966
